title: Publicly verifiable unclonable money and copy-protected programs

concept.text: The proposed innovation would turn quantum information into reusable objects that people can use and authenticate but cannot feasibly duplicate. For money, a mint would issue a quantum banknote with an authenticated serial number, and anyone with the public verification procedure could check it without contacting the mint. Security would mean that an efficient quantum adversary holding a valid note has only negligible probability of turning it into two notes accepted for that serial number. This extends the historical private-key quantum-money model, in which the mint must participate in verification.

For software, the corresponding object would be a quantum state that lets its holder evaluate a specified program repeatedly while resisting conversion into additional independently useful implementations. Decryption and signing programs are proposed targets, but the protected program family and its security game must be explicit. Money and software protection share the aim of preventing duplication, yet they require different definitions and constructions; achieving either capability would not automatically establish the other.

The no-cloning principle provides a physical basis for this goal, but it does not itself prove that a counterfeiter cannot manufacture two objects that pass a particular verifier or perform well enough in a program challenge. The intended advance therefore combines cryptographic security with reliable quantum storage and operation. It is a proposed capability, not a demonstrated practical system in the supplied evidence.

significance.text: Classical digital tokens can be copied, so preventing double spending requires mechanisms beyond possession of a bit string. A secure, publicly verifiable quantum banknote could support bearer payments without an online mint or a transaction ledger: the recipient would authenticate the transferred quantum object itself. This is a conditional consequence of the proposed construction, not evidence of a deployed payment system. It would not eliminate issuance, public-key authentication, or the other infrastructure needed to operate a monetary system.

Copy-protected quantum programs would create a different way to distribute executable capabilities. A holder could use a protected implementation without gaining the ability to issue arbitrarily many additional working implementations. Classical obfuscation may conceal aspects of a program, but its classical output remains copyable; it does not by itself provide this property. The potential advance is nevertheless class-specific: some programs that cannot be learned from their input-output behavior still cannot be copy-protected. Unlearnability is therefore insufficient to justify a claim of general software protection.

Conditional downstream possibilities include distributing limited quantities of decryption or signing capabilities and transferring digital bearer assets without recording every transfer centrally. These possibilities would depend on the exact security definitions, supported program families, and usable lifetime of the quantum states. They are proposed applications, not established consequences for every cryptographic task or every deployment.

The analogy with physical cash or a limited-copy software license has practical limits. Quantum objects must survive storage, transfer, and repeated verification or evaluation. A cryptographic proof against efficient adversaries does not guarantee an unlimited physical lifetime or resistance to every implementation flaw. Those engineering requirements would determine whether the theoretical capability becomes useful outside a controlled setting.

missing_breakthrough.text: The cryptographic challenge is to obtain convincing public verification and resistance to counterfeiting with clearly stated assumptions and a security model that does not depend on an idealized oracle. Two distinctions matter: a standard-model proof avoids such idealized access, whereas a proof from standard, well-studied assumptions concerns the credibility of its foundation. A construction can satisfy the first description while relying on a nonstandard assumption. The supplied group-action work illustrates this distinction through generic-model security and an alternative standard-model argument involving a knowledge assumption whose soundness needs further analysis.

For software, the missing capability is reusable protection for a useful, explicitly identified program family under an appropriate duplication game. The challenge includes defining what counts as an independently successful implementation and how success is measured on challenge inputs. Protection must remain meaningful when an adversary obtains multiple legitimate program states. Best-possible protection does not mean that every program becomes protectable; known unlearnable counterexamples rule out that interpretation.

Obfuscation does not provide an unrestricted route around the money problem. The supplied 2025 barrier concerns black-box constructions from obfuscation for evasive functions when the mint makes classical obfuscation queries and the verifier makes only evaluation queries, with no obfuscation queries. A successful approach would have to avoid the covered setting or use a different foundation. The result does not establish that every obfuscation-based construction, or public quantum money itself, is impossible.

Engineering synthesis: a practical construction would also need a specified device and noise model, sufficiently reliable preparation and storage, transfer of quantum states, and repeated operations that preserve honest usability. Its proof would need to accommodate whatever errors and acceptance tolerances the implementation permits. The supplied evidence does not resolve the resource requirements or demonstrate this combination on hardware.

current_state.text: Private-key quantum money dates to Wiesner: in that model the mint verifies banknotes and must participate in transactions. Public-key quantum money changes the verification role so that anyone can authenticate a note while issuance remains controlled by the mint. This historical distinction establishes the target capability, not the present-day availability or absence of a practical implementation.

Mark Zhandry’s Quantum Money from Abelian Group Actions, published in TheoretiCS on 19 August 2025, constructs public-key quantum money and quantum lightning from abelian group actions. The supplied review identifies security in the generic group-action model under a new computational assumption. The work does not establish security from standard isogeny assumptions. It also discusses an alternative standard-model argument using a nonstandard knowledge assumption whose soundness requires further analysis. Thus, describing all of its security arguments as outside the standard model would omit a material qualification.

Andrea Coladangelo and Sam Gunn’s How to Use Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation, in the supplied arXiv version dated 3 May 2024, shows that the quantum obfuscation notion qsiO achieves best-possible copy protection and constructs qsiO relative to an efficient quantum oracle. It also gives conditional copy-protection results for specified puncturable programs, including a signing-function example discussed in the review. Best-possible protection preserves protection where it is possible; it does not overcome the existence of programs that cannot be protected. The oracle construction and conditional results do not establish a practical, general-purpose implementation.

The same 2024 source describes standard-model unclonable encryption as an open problem at that time. Unclonable encryption is a separate primitive, so that statement cannot establish that publicly verifiable quantum money is absent in the standard model, much less that no noisy-device implementation exists.

Zhandry’s On Quantum Money and Evasive Obfuscation, identified in the supplied research as EUROCRYPT 2025 and IACR ePrint 2025/325, supplies a black-box barrier under the mint and verifier restrictions described above. The retained evidence is the ePrint landing-page abstract, not the full paper. It supports that bounded barrier statement, but does not support extending the impossibility to constructions outside its stated query restrictions.

The supplied review found no demonstration in the retained texts of a noise-tolerant, standard-model, publicly verifiable banknote on specified hardware. That observation has limited scope: both arXiv extractions were truncated at 120,000 characters, and the supplied freshness search record is empty. The dated theoretical results remain supported, but the inputs do not establish a comprehensive state-of-the-field assessment as of 1 November 2026. Missing evidence here is not proof that an unexamined result is false or nonexistent.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed money criterion: specify a mint, an authenticated serial-number mechanism, a public verifier, a device class, and a noise model. Demonstrate reliable honest-note acceptance and reusable verification, with explicit bounds on degradation over storage, transfer, and repeated checks. Provide a standard-model reduction to a named assumption showing that an efficient quantum adversary given one valid note has only negligible probability of producing two notes accepted for that note’s authenticated serial number. State the assumption’s maturity separately from the proof’s standard-model status.
completion_criteria.label: Standard-model proof of negligible one-to-two counterfeiting for reusable public money

completion_criteria.text: Proposed money extension: define and prove security for the intended multiple-note setting, including the adversary’s access to legitimately issued notes and verification procedures. A one-note experiment alone would not establish security for a circulation system with many notes. Experiments should measure honest acceptance, lifetime, operating costs, and performance within the declared noise envelope; a failure to counterfeit in laboratory trials would complement, rather than replace, the computational proof.
completion_criteria.label: Multiple-note circulation security proved under declared adversarial access

completion_criteria.text: Proposed software criterion: identify a family of decryption or signing programs, its allowed uses, and a challenge distribution. Supply reusable evaluation on the specified device class and prove that an adversary with any polynomial number of legitimately issued program states cannot obtain more independently successful implementations than authorized. Here, collusion without a fixed copy bound means coverage of polynomially many copies within the formal security model; it does not mean unlimited computation or unrestricted access. Honest correctness, evaluation lifetime, and success measures must be explicit.
completion_criteria.label: Reusable programs resist polynomial-copy collusion producing excess successful implementations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility criterion: make the construction, security definitions, assumptions, proof, and implementation details available for independent examination, then reproduce the claimed operation and noise tolerance independently. Report concrete resource costs and the boundary beyond which reliability or security claims no longer apply. No numerical acceptance rate, lifetime, or overhead threshold is established by the supplied evidence, so these would need to be justified for the intended application.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction reports noise tolerance, resource costs, and claim boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Under this proposed completion target, a generic-group proof or protection restricted to point functions would constitute partial progress. A named useful program family could satisfy the software target without protecting all programs. Finite demonstrations would establish tested breadth, device compatibility, and operating limits; they would not establish literal universality or replace a theorem for the declared family. These criteria are proposals, not established field standards.
completion_criteria.label: State program-family security scope and limits of finite demonstrations

related_concepts.text: CRY-03, Practically efficient post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation, has the closest methodological overlap. Obfuscation appears in both conditional copy-protection constructions and the evasive-obfuscation barrier for money. However, quantum obfuscation notions used in the supplied copy-protection work should not be equated automatically with an efficient classical post-quantum obfuscator. A copyable classical obfuscation does not itself become an unclonable program state, and the money barrier applies only within its specified black-box setting.

Roster comparison, offered as synthesis: CRY-01, A proof that an explicit one-way function exists, and CRY-02, Public-key encryption from one-way functions, concern foundational existence and construction questions. CRY-05 instead concerns preventing duplication of usable quantum objects. A theorem about one-way functions or encryption would not by itself supply public banknote verification or protected quantum programs. Unclonable encryption is an additional nearby primitive, distinct from both ordinary encryption and public quantum money.

Roster comparison, offered as synthesis: CRY-04, General-purpose private computation at near-plaintext cost, aims to protect information during computation, while CRY-05 aims to limit duplication of executable capabilities or banknotes. CRY-08, Metadata-private messaging at ordinary cost, concerns communication privacy. Neither privacy goal follows automatically from unclonability: a publicly verifiable note need not provide transaction anonymity, and a copy-protected program need not conceal every aspect of its use.

Roster comparison, offered as synthesis: CRY-06, Practical classical verification of quantum computation, concerns checking quantum computational work using a classical verifier. CRY-05 concerns authenticating a quantum object and preventing its duplication; public verification does not imply that verification is entirely classical. CRY-07, Position verification that works in physical spacetime, concerns authenticating location under physical and adversarial constraints. It shares a need to align cryptographic models with physical capabilities, but location authentication and unclonable ownership remain distinct goals.

Roster comparison, offered as synthesis: CRY-09, Post-quantum timed release with a sequentiality theorem, controls when information becomes accessible rather than how many usable copies exist. CRY-10, A conclusive quantum classification of deployed lattice encryption, evaluates the security of a particular family of assumptions against quantum attack. Such assumption analysis would be relevant if a CRY-05 construction depended on those assumptions, but no such dependency is established in the supplied record.

Quantum lightning is a nearby primitive explicitly constructed alongside public quantum money in the supplied group-action work. Its appearance in the same research connects the two directions, but it does not establish the software-protection component of CRY-05 or the device-level completion criteria proposed here.

change_log.reason: They share an unclonability objective but require different security definitions; success for one does not automatically establish the other.

change_log.change: Replaced absolute claims that nobody can duplicate the objects with computational security against efficient quantum adversaries.
change_log.reason: No-cloning alone does not establish the relevant counterfeiting or program-duplication guarantees.

change_log.change: Restricted the software impact to specified protectable program families and explained the limits of best-possible protection.
change_log.reason: The reviewed source explicitly identifies unlearnable programs that cannot be copy-protected.

change_log.change: Separated standard-model proofs from proofs based on standard, well-studied assumptions and restored the alternative knowledge-assumption argument.
change_log.reason: The group-action source discusses a standard-model route under a nonstandard knowledge assumption, so the original blanket description was incomplete.

change_log.change: Removed unclonable encryption’s historical open-problem statement as evidence for the absence of public quantum money.
change_log.reason: The statement concerns a distinct primitive and cannot establish the broader money or hardware claim.

change_log.change: Restored the requirement that the mint’s obfuscation queries are classical in the evasive-obfuscation barrier.
change_log.reason: Together with evaluation-only verification, this materially limits the scope of the impossibility result.

change_log.change: Retained the dated theoretical achievements while qualifying hardware absence and present-day openness.
change_log.reason: The review relied on truncated arXiv extractions, an abstract-only ePrint page, and an empty freshness record.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed completion criteria to include honest correctness, authenticated serial numbers, reusable operation, multiple-note security, collusion definitions, and independent reproduction.
change_log.reason: These details make the proposed breakthrough assessable without treating an experiment as a security proof or presenting proposed thresholds as consensus standards.

unresolved_issues: The supplied inputs do not establish the complete state of public quantum money or copy protection as of 1 November 2026; no freshness search results were supplied.
Both arXiv extractions were truncated at 120,000 characters. The retained ePrint evidence is a landing-page abstract, leaving full technical details beyond those reviewed unestablished here.
The soundness and suitability of the nonstandard knowledge assumption used in the alternative standard-model money argument require further analysis.
No specific decryption or signing family, challenge distribution, or multiple-copy security theorem is selected as the final software target.
Device resources, noise tolerances, usable lifetimes, transfer requirements, and practical acceptance thresholds remain unspecified and are not demonstrated by the supplied evidence.
The intended relationship between public verification, serial-number authentication, and supporting issuance infrastructure must be made concrete in an eventual construction.

brief.title: Money and programs that people cannot copy
possible: You could receive a digital banknote and check it yourself without contacting its issuer or consulting a transaction ledger. The note would be stored as quantum information, a physical state whose duplication can be restricted by physics and cryptography.
You could repeatedly use a protected program to unlock encrypted messages or sign documents, while being unable to turn it into extra working copies.
why: Recipients could authenticate money as it changes hands without centrally recording every payment. Software providers could distribute limited quantities of working programs while giving holders repeated use.

sources.showed: Zhandry constructed publicly checkable quantum money. Its main security proof uses an idealized mathematical model and a new assumption. An alternative proof avoids that model but relies on an assumption whose soundness needs further analysis.
sources.quote: We prove security in the generic group model for group actions under a plausible computational assumption
sources.cited_for: The work supplies a theoretical construction of money that anyone can authenticate.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a working banknote that tolerates hardware errors or security based on well-studied assumptions.

sources.showed: They proved that quantum obfuscation, which conceals a program's implementation, preserves copy protection wherever protection is possible. They constructed it with access to an idealized quantum helper and gave conditional results for specified program families.
sources.quote: As our first contribution, we show how to achieve “best-possible” copy protection for all programs.
sources.cited_for: The work provides a conditional route to protecting reusable programs against copying.
sources.not_established: It does not provide a practical implementation, and some programs cannot be protected against copying.

sources.showed: Zhandry proved that a restricted route from obfuscation to public quantum money fails. The result depends on how the issuer and checker may access the underlying tools.
sources.quote: We show a black box barrier against constructing public key quantum money from obfuscation for evasive functions.
sources.cited_for: The result rules out a specified approach to constructing publicly checkable quantum money.
sources.not_established: The barrier leaves approaches outside its access restrictions unresolved.

shown: Zhandry has constructed theoretical quantum money with public checking and conditional security proofs. Coladangelo and Gunn have established conditional protection for specified kinds of programs. Their construction uses an idealized quantum helper.
These results establish mathematical progress. Combining the proofs with reliable storage, transfer and repeated operation on specified hardware remains a separate challenge.
missing: Publicly checkable money still needs a convincing security proof without idealized helpers, alongside reliable operation under a stated error model.
A useful program family needs reusable protection that remains secure when attackers combine many legitimately issued copies.
A practical system needs reliable quantum storage, transfer and repeated use, with measured lifetimes and resource costs.

milestones.label: Reusable money with a counterfeiting proof
milestones.explanation: A proof without idealized helpers would have to bound an efficient attacker's chance of duplicating a valid note, alongside reliable repeated checks under stated hardware errors. This would establish the basic money capability.

milestones.label: Security during circulation of many notes
milestones.explanation: A proof would have to cover attackers accessing many legitimate notes and checks, with experiments measuring reliability, lifetime and costs. This would extend the claim to circulation.

milestones.label: Reusable programs resist attacks combining legitimate copies
milestones.explanation: A named program family would need reliable repeated use and a proof against producing excess working copies from any efficiently growing supply of authorized copies. This would establish protection against coordinated copying.

milestones.label: Independent reproduction with measured costs and error tolerance
milestones.explanation: Independent researchers would have to reproduce the claimed operation and error tolerance using disclosed construction and proof details, reporting costs and limits. This would establish reproducibility and practical requirements.

milestones.label: A defined scope for program protection
milestones.explanation: The result would have to identify the useful program family covered by its proof and the limits of finite demonstrations. This would establish which software the protection actually covers.

uncertain: The soundness of the alternative money proof's new knowledge assumption remains open to further analysis.
The target program family and the tests defining successful unauthorized copies still need to be chosen.
Required hardware resources, error tolerance, usable lifetimes and practical acceptance thresholds remain unspecified.

page.title: Public-key quantum money and copy-protected decryption keys
page.definition: A mint issues quantum banknotes that recipients can authenticate with a public key and pass on for another payment. Stored optical notes have been checked with the issuing bank’s secret record. A copy-protected quantum decryption key lets its holder repeatedly recover messages from ciphertexts. In each scheme, an efficient quantum adversary’s probability of producing more accepted notes or working decryptors than it received must be negligible: eventually smaller than every inverse polynomial in the security parameter λ.

goal.need: Cash recipients check printed security features by sight and touch. In 2025, 14 counterfeit euro notes were detected per million genuine notes in circulation. Merchants with quantum verifiers could authenticate a note locally and spend it again, provided its quantum state survives between payments. Software vendors could give several customers reusable decryption keys without enabling them to pool their keys and equip another user. A customer given a classical key can copy it regardless of its length.

statements.quote: Achieving secure software copy protection is one of our goals.
anyone (with a quantum computer) can verify that the state came from the mint without sending the money back to the mint.
statements.context: Abstract of Shor’s colloquium hosted by NIST on 21 January 2011; this is the speaker’s statement.

statements.quote: Here, we will study and implement one of the most promising quantum applications, namely unforgeable quantum money.

statements.body: Swiss National Bank and Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts, Practical Central Bank Quantum Money
statements.context: The project calls for central-bank issuance and distribution to consumers through retail banks. Its deliverables include a cryptographic protocol, a security analysis and an implementation plan.

completion.title: Public quantum money and reusable decryption-key copy protection satisfy their security games on hardware.
completion.criterion: Physical implementations of public-key quantum money and reusable quantum decryption keys meet their published games without idealized oracles. Honest operation succeeds with probability ≥1−negl(λ) through polynomially many uses. No polynomial-time quantum adversary can turn q issued notes into >q accepted notes except negligibly, for any polynomial q; from any polynomial k decryption keys, its probability of passing the joint (k+1)-decryptor projective threshold test at 1/2+γ is negligible for every inverse-polynomial γ>0. Proofs cover the implementations’ stated noise models under explicit computational assumptions.
completion.set_by: Atlas; joint physical-realisation test combining Aaronson–Christiano’s money definition and Çakan–Goyal’s decryption-key protection definition.
completion.basis: No joint hardware completion test was found in NIST’s quantum-money material, ANR quBIC, NTT’s goal statement, or the cited money and copy-protection definitions. Atlas combines their two capabilities and requires physical operation of both. The component games supply the security thresholds; no transaction-rate or storage-lifetime target is added. Conditional circuit constructions alone do not meet this physical test.

milestones.title: Stored private-key quantum money operates inside its proved noise-and-loss security region.
milestones.criterion: Store and retrieve polarization-encoded weak coherent pulses for one round of bank-assisted verification. The storage-and-retrieval efficiency η must exceed 50%, and the measured error rate must fall below the Figure 2 security boundary for that η and mean photon number per pulse μ.
milestones.set_by: Mamann et al., Wiesner-money protocol security analysis, Figure 2 and Supplementary Text; this threshold is for private-key verification.
milestones.threshold_quote: We first observe that, owing to the no-cloning theorem, an efficiency above 50% is required to have a possible range of secure operations.

milestones.title: A public-money mini-scheme limits one-to-two counterfeiting to negligible probability.
milestones.criterion: Every valid note must be accepted with probability at least 2/3. Given one freshly issued note, any polynomial-size quantum circuit has negligible probability of producing two states that both pass public verification for that note’s serial number. The two output states may be entangled. The probability is over issuance, the circuit and both verification measurements.
milestones.set_by: Aaronson and Christiano, Definition 12; the security convention used for public-money mini-schemes.
milestones.threshold_quote: We call M secure if it has completeness error ≤ 1/3 and negligible soundness error.

milestones.title: Quantum state obfuscation preserves every attainable two-output copy-protection security bound.
milestones.criterion: Fix a family of classical circuits, a verification procedure and a bound δ(λ) already attainable by copy protection for that family. Obfuscation must preserve honest evaluation. For a uniformly sampled circuit given in obfuscated form, any quantum polynomial-time adversary has probability at most δ(λ) plus a negligible term of producing two implementations that both pass the specified verifier, even when their states are entangled.
milestones.set_by: Coladangelo and Gunn, Definition 4 and Theorem 1; Theorem 2 supplies an oracle construction.
milestones.threshold_quote: Then, $\mathsf{qsiO}$ is a $(\Ver,\delta)$-secure copy protection scheme for $\calF$.

milestones.title: A public-money mini-scheme accepts all tolerated errors with negligible counterfeiting probability.
milestones.criterion: Relative to the classical oracle, use an n/2-dimensional binary subspace C of length n with both C and its dual of distance at least 2q+1, for q≥1. Verification must accept with probability 1 after any Pauli error X^e Z^e′ in E, where each error string has at most q nonzero entries. Given one freshly minted note, an efficient quantum adversary’s probability of producing two accepted states for its serial number is at most |E|²/exp(n). Choose parameters for which this bound is negligible.
milestones.set_by: Peter Yuen, Definitions 3.3–3.4, Equation 29 and Theorem 4.10.
milestones.threshold_quote: has perfect completeness and $|\mathcal{E}|^{2}/\textsf{exp}(n)$ soundness error.

milestones.title: Reusable decryption keys resist k-to-k+1 piracy for every polynomial number k of issued keys.
milestones.criterion: In the plain model, honest decryption must succeed with probability 1 and permit reuse of the key. Give a quantum polynomial-time adversary the public key and generate a fresh quantum decryption key for each query. Setup takes no collusion bound. After k queries the adversary supplies k+1 candidate decryptors and a challenge message pair for each. For every inverse-polynomial γ>0, the probability that all k+1 pass their projective threshold tests for distinguishing honest encryptions at 1/2+γ must be negligible.
milestones.set_by: Çakan and Goyal, Definitions 23 and 26, Theorem 32 and Corollary 6; extends prior anti-piracy games.
milestones.threshold_quote: PKE satisfies strong γ-anti-piracy for any inverse polynomial γ.

milestones.title: Physical public quantum money permits repeated checking and resists q-to-more-than-q counterfeiting.
milestones.criterion: A physical implementation supplies minting and reusable public verification, with every oracle replaced by explicit algorithms. Under its stated noise model, honest acceptance is ≥1−negl(λ) through polynomially many checks; any polynomial-time quantum adversary given q=poly(λ) issued notes produces >q accepted notes only with negligible probability.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; hardware extension of Aaronson–Christiano Definition 11 and Appendix 9; no hardware acceptance protocol found in NIST, ANR quBIC or NTT goals.

milestones.title: An optical banknote passes the bank’s polarization-fidelity test.
milestones.criterion: Prepare a sequence of single-photon polarization states and measure each in the basis recorded by the bank. The fraction of conclusive projections that give the expected state must exceed the mean verification fidelity F̄pass calibrated for the preparation distribution and the verifier’s resolution. This tests authentication of the prepared sequence.
milestones.set_by: Bartkiewicz et al., optical banknote verification rule following Equation 12.
milestones.threshold_quote: A quantum banknote passes the verification process if $\bar{F}_{i}>\bar{F}_{\mathrm{pass}}.$

milestones.title: With k fixed at setup, k decryption keys resist conversion into k+1 working decryptors.
milestones.criterion: For any polynomial bound k supplied at setup, give a quantum polynomial-time adversary the public key and all k quantum decryption keys. It chooses a pair of distinct messages and outputs k+1 possibly entangled decryptors. For every inverse-polynomial γ>0, the probability that all k+1 pass the 1/2+γ threshold test for distinguishing encryptions of that message pair must be negligible.
milestones.set_by: Liu, Liu, Qian and Zhandry, Definitions 3.1 and 3.3–3.5 and Theorem 3.6.
milestones.threshold_quote: The challenger outputs 1 if and only if all the measurements output 1.

not_found: No joint hardware acceptance criterion was found in the NIST, ANR quBIC or NTT material.
No physical public-money system meeting m6, or physical reusable decryption-key system meeting the completion criterion, was located.
The Wiesner Labs prize page yielded no readable rules.

results.finding: Abelian group action quantum money has negligible joint acceptance probability for two outputs from one freshly minted note.
results.detail: The proof uses the interactive D2X/min assumption and generic group action labels of length m′ ≥ 2m + ω(log λ). The paper flags that its lightning definition excludes nonuniform attackers with hard-coded quantum advice.
results.quote: Then the quantum money construction is a secure quantum lightning scheme.

results.finding: An ideal abelian group action banknote passes each public check with probability 1 and remains intact.
results.detail: The repeat-check result follows from the exact projection in Theorem 3.2. The generic counterfeiting proof uses an idealized group action oracle.
results.quote: In particular, honest banknotes are accepted with probability 1.

results.finding: For one uniformly sampled obfuscated classical circuit, the probability that both candidate implementations pass is at most δ(λ) + negl(λ).
results.detail: Theorem 1 assumes a secure obfuscator and an existing copy-protection scheme for the same verifier and bound. Equation (7) omits δ(λ). Definition 4 supplies the δ(λ) + negl(λ) bound required by the reduction.

results.detail: The fidelity result comes from the no-storage measurements. The vendor chose the basis randomly, and the bank excluded basis mismatches during verification.

results.finding: Stored optical banknotes had a 0.78% verification error rate at μ = 1 for a 28-state sequence repeated 4,000 times.
results.detail: The reported efficiency is an average across μ = 0.5, 1, 1.5, and 2. The bank verified detections in matching bases using its secret record.

results.finding: Given one issued Fourier-state banknote, a polynomial-size quantum counterfeiter has negligible probability of getting two outputs accepted for its serial number.
results.detail: Theorems 4.8 and 5.1 establish security in the generic group action model under the group-action discrete logarithm hardness assumption. The proof relies on smooth group order.
results.quote:
Our main result is a quantum polynomial-time reduction from the group action discrete
logarithm (DLP) problem to a specific cloning problem. A consequence of this result is that the
public-key quantum money scheme proposed by Zhandry (2024), which is based on abelian group
actions, is secure in the generic group action model.

results.finding: Non-Abelian public quantum money with one freshly minted note has negligible probability of two accepted outputs under preaction security.
results.detail: The result is conditional on preaction security. The excerpt gives a plain-model reduction and presents the McEliece-based group action as a candidate for the assumption.
results.quote:
We show below
that if the group action is preaction secure, then the quantum money construction satisfies lightning
security.

results.finding: For each valid note, uncomputing a public verification check restores the original state with probability 1 in the ideal circuit model.
results.detail: The verifier checks the irreducible-representation label and leaves the other Fourier indices unmeasured so it can reverse the circuit.
results.quote:
However, the resulting modified banknote will also be valid for the same serial number, and
furthermore, the circuit can be uncomputed to return the original banknote.

results.finding: Reusable public-key decryption keys: from any polynomial k issued keys, the joint pass probability for k+1 candidate decryptors is negligible.
results.detail: Theorem 1 states the existence result. Sections 2.1 and 2.2 describe the construction and projective threshold game, with the full security proof referenced in Section 7.3.
results.quote:
Theorem 1. Assuming post-quantum subexponentially secure indisting uishability obfuscation and
subexponentially secure L WE, there exists a public-key enc ryption scheme with fully collusion-
resistant copy-protected secret keys.

results.finding: Public quantum coins from 1 issued coin have negligible joint acceptance probability for 2 counterfeit outputs.
results.detail: The compiled coins contain superpositions of signed mini-banknotes. Their public verifier checks the serial number carried by each branch rather than testing both outputs against one serial number supplied at issuance.
results.quote: is a quantum coin scheme that satisfies correctness and unclonability (counterfeiting) security.

results.finding: For any polynomial q of issued public quantum coins, the probability of producing q+1 jointly accepted coins is negligible.
results.detail: Theorem 11 and Corollary 3 give the plain-model construction. Coherent verification and rewinding preserve honest coins in the ideal model.
results.quote: Assuming the existence of subspace-hiding obfuscation and one-way functions, there exists a public-key quantum coin scheme.

results.finding: Multi-copy SDE is reported for any polynomial k exact key copies in the k-to-(k+1) security setting.

title = "Public-key quantum money and copy-protected decryption keys". Reason: The title currently covers software families beyond the decryption keys specified by the completion test.

definition = "A mint issues quantum banknotes that recipients can authenticate with a public key and pass on for another payment. Stored optical notes have been checked with the issuing bank\u2019s secret record. A copy-protected quantum decryption key lets its holder repeatedly recover messages from ciphertexts. In each scheme, an efficient quantum adversary\u2019s probability of producing more accepted notes or working decryptors than it received must be negligible: eventually smaller than every inverse polynomial in the security parameter \u03bb.". Reason: The definition needs to distinguish a recipient’s public check from the bank-assisted optical demonstration and identify the decryption key as the protected object.

goal.need = "Cash recipients check printed security features by sight and touch. In 2025, 14 counterfeit euro notes were detected per million genuine notes in circulation. Merchants with quantum verifiers could authenticate a note locally and spend it again, provided its quantum state survives between payments. Software vendors could give several customers reusable decryption keys without enabling them to pool their keys and equip another user. A customer given a classical key can copy it regardless of its length.". Reason: The current rationale gives a security game and a laboratory result but omits the scale of counterfeiting and the benefit to vendors who issue keys to several customers.

add statement by Swiss National Bank and Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts, Practical Central Bank Quantum Money, 2025: "a viable quantum money scheme". Reason: The Swiss project adds a central bank’s stated goal and identifies the distribution requirement that a banknote protocol must meet in its monetary system.

add milestone after None: "An optical banknote passes the bank’s polarization-fidelity test.". Reason: The first listed laboratory test requires a memory, although the earlier optical banknote experiment already tested authentication against a calibrated fidelity threshold.

edit m1: criterion = "Store and retrieve polarization-encoded weak coherent pulses for one round of bank-assisted verification. The storage-and-retrieval efficiency \u03b7 must exceed 50%, and the measured error rate must fall below the Figure 2 security boundary for that \u03b7 and mean photon number per pulse \u03bc.". Reason: The criterion mixes the protocol’s error and efficiency limits with the date, repetition count and outcome of one experiment.

edit m2: criterion = "Every valid note must be accepted with probability at least 2/3. Given one freshly issued note, any polynomial-size quantum circuit has negligible probability of producing two states that both pass public verification for that note\u2019s serial number. The two output states may be entangled. The probability is over issuance, the circuit and both verification measurements."; refs = [6]. Reason: The mini-scheme definition gives one double-verification test independent of the papers, proof models and publication dates currently listed in its criterion.

edit m3: criterion = "Fix a family of classical circuits, a verification procedure and a bound \u03b4(\u03bb) already attainable by copy protection for that family. Obfuscation must preserve honest evaluation. For a uniformly sampled circuit given in obfuscated form, any quantum polynomial-time adversary has probability at most \u03b4(\u03bb) plus a negligible term of producing two implementations that both pass the specified verifier, even when their states are entangled.". Reason: The criterion needs the conditions of the two-output game in place of the publication history of the obfuscation theorem.

edit m4: title = "A public-money mini-scheme accepts all tolerated errors with negligible counterfeiting probability."; criterion = "Relative to the classical oracle, use an n/2-dimensional binary subspace C of length n with both C and its dual of distance at least 2q+1, for q\u22651.
